title: How the Translators Changed the Text
kicker: The Recursive I Ching · from Bouvet to the bronze-age translations
description: Every translation of the I Ching is also an edition: it chooses a Chinese text, decides where the commentaries go, and brings the questions of its century. This course follows those choices.
intro:
A translation of the I Ching makes at least three choices before it translates a word. Which Chinese text (in practice, until the tombs were opened, the Song reading in the Kangxi edition ◇)? Where do the Ten Wings go: apart, as Legge printed them, or woven into each hexagram, as Wilhelm did? And whose questions does it bring? Jesuits looked for the Bible, Leibniz for binary numbers, Victorians for a scripture to set beside their own, Jung for synchronicity, and the bronze-age translators for a Zhou diviner.

One word shows how much rides on those choices. Zhen (貞) closes many judgments. In the oracle bones it means 'to divine'; the Han commentators read it as 'correct'; Legge gives 'firm and correct', and the recent translations try 'divining' again [@wp_iching]. ✔ The same line can be advice about virtue or a note that a question was put to the stalks.

This library reads Legge, because his translation is in the public domain. In September 2026 it found Wilhelm/Baynes wording, still in copyright, in one of its grammars and replaced it; that story is in the Baynes chapter [@repo_changelog].
